zh-TW.title: 閉包：函式的隨身背包
zh-TW.question: 外層函式都跑完了，裡面的變數怎麼還在？
zh-TW.answer: 函式被帶走時，會把當下看得到的變數一起留住。就算外層已經結束，你還是**能讀、也能改**它。

steps.lead: 交出去的函式，還抓著外層的 `count`
steps.body: `increment` 就寫在 `createCounter` 裡面，天生看得到 `count`。就算 `createCounter` 跑完收工了，只要 `increment` 還在你手上，這條連線就不會斷。函式加上它留住的變數，就是閉包。

notes.text: 每次呼叫 `createCounter`，都會準備一個**全新的** `count`。
`increment` 寫在裡面，天生看得到這個 `count`。
這裡只先拿到函式，還沒呼叫它，所以 `count` 停在 0。

analogy.title: 像留著備份鑰匙
analogy.text: 鐵門拉下來了，工具還在裡面；鑰匙在你口袋，隨時能開門進去用。

recall.question: `createCounter()` 跑完之後，`count` 為什麼沒被清掉？
recall.answer: 還有人用得到它。交出去的 `increment` 還抓著 `count`，所以記憶體不會清掉。
recall.hint: 想想看，現在誰手上還握著 `count`？

steps.lead: 留住的是變數本人，不是當下的快照
steps.body: 每次呼叫 `counter()`，你改到的都是同一個 `count`。閉包留住的是「走回那個變數的路」，不是建立那一刻拍下的死數字。看 `count` 欄，數字會一路往上接。

figure.caption: 看 count 欄：每次呼叫都接著上一次的數字往上加。

deeper.summary: 別處改了變數，閉包看到的也會變
deeper.body: 閉包握著的是通往外層變數的連線，不是複製一份出來。如果同一個外層裡還有別的函式把 `count` 改成 100，你下一次呼叫 `counter()` 就會拿到 101。這也是以前在 `for` 迴圈裡用 `var` 常踩坑的原因：好幾個函式抓到同一個變數，最後印出來全是迴圈跑完的終點值。

recall.question: 建立 `counter` 後連續呼叫三次，第三次會回傳多少？
recall.answer: 3。三次呼叫改的都是同一個 `count`，會從 2 再往上加 1。
recall.hint: 這三次呼叫改到的，是不是同一個 `count`？

steps.lead: 再呼叫一次工廠，就會分到全新的背包
steps.body: 再跑一次 `createCounter(10)`，就會生出另一個獨立的 `count`。`anotherCounter` 從 10 起跳，不管你按幾次，都不會動到原本 `counter` 裡面的數字。

figure.verdict: 長得一模一樣，但各自的 `count` 互不干擾。

analogy.title: 像同一本記帳格
analogy.text: 影印給兩家便當店，欄位一樣，但帳各記各的。

recall.question: 分別建立的兩個計數器，會共用同一個 `count` 嗎？
recall.answer: 不會。每次呼叫 `createCounter` 都會生出獨立的 `count`，兩邊各算各的。
recall.hint: 每次呼叫 `createCounter`，第 2 行做了什麼？

followUps: 為什麼把 `createCounter()` 寫在點擊事件裡，數字永遠停在 1？
想同時提供 `increment` 和 `reset`，怎麼讓它們共用同一個 `count`？

source.label: JavaScript 閉包與獨立計數器

en.title: Closures: A Function's Backpack
en.question: Why does a returned function still remember `count`?
en.answer: A function keeps a live link to variables where it was born. You can **read and update** them.

steps.lead: The returned function keeps a live link to `count`
steps.body: `increment` lives inside `createCounter`, so `count` is naturally in reach. Even after `createCounter` finishes, holding onto `increment` keeps that link alive. A function plus the variables it holds onto is a closure.

notes.text: `increment` is defined inside, so `count` stays in reach.
`counter` holds the function itself; `count` is still 0.

analogy.title: Like a spare key
analogy.text: The shop closed, tools stay inside, and your key still works.

recall.question: Why isn't `count` cleared when `createCounter()` ends?
recall.answer: Because `increment` still uses it. Memory keeps a variable alive as long as a function holds onto it.
recall.hint: Which function still has a hand on `count`?

steps.lead: It keeps the variable itself, not a frozen snapshot
steps.body: Every `counter()` call updates that same `count`. A closure keeps a path back to the variable, not a photo taken when it was created. Watch the `count` column build on each call.

figure.caption: Watch `count`: each call picks up from the previous value.

deeper.summary: Outside edits show up inside, too
deeper.body: A closure holds a live reference, not a private copy. If another function in the same outer scope sets `count` to 100, the next `counter()` call returns 101. That is why `var` inside a `for` loop trips people up: every callback shares one variable and reads its final loop value.

recall.question: Call a fresh `counter()` three times. What prints third?
recall.answer: 3. All three calls update the same `count`, stepping it from 2 to 3.
recall.hint: Are all three calls touching the same `count`?

steps.lead: Every factory call hands out a brand-new backpack
steps.body: Calling `createCounter(10)` spins up a separate `count`. `anotherCounter` starts at 10, and calling it all day never touches the `count` inside `counter`.

figure.verdict: Same blueprint, separate `count` variables, zero overlap.

analogy.title: Like a template
analogy.text: Print two copies for two shops; each tracks its own tabs.

recall.question: Do `counter` and `anotherCounter` share the same `count`?
recall.answer: No. Each `createCounter` call creates its own `count`, so the two counters stay independent.
recall.hint: What does line 2 do each time `createCounter` runs?
